World.title: Burnham will divert ‘significant’ resources out of civil service, says No. 10 North chief
World.content:
Burnham’s Cabinet signed a statement last month which said No. 10 North would oversee a “major transfer of powers, resources and functions” from central to local government before the next general election, due by 2029. It promised to “build new career paths between central government and the wider public sector” and make the civil service “smaller and more strategic.”

Britain’s civil service has ballooned by 100,000 people in six years to around 550,000 following the Covid-19 pandemic and the U.K.’s exit from the European Union.

Simpson declined to say to what extent the overall headcount of civil servants will be cut to increase staffing in regional government. “I am not going to put a figure on what that is going to look like,” she said.

However, she added: “The intent behind [the Cabinet paper] — really moving significant resource from Whitehall and from the civil service into regions, into local areas — is absolutely part of our plan, our ambition, our mission here in No. 10 North.”

Burnham has said he wants all areas of England to have mayoral authorities in place by the end of 2028, and they are set to be offered the expertise of Whitehall officials where it is relevant and desired.

It is not yet clear how this movement of staff will work in practice. Officials plan to outline more detail in a paper alongside the Oct. 26 budget, which — as with a spending review in 2027 — will make clear the impact on Whitehall budgets.

World.title: The drone war is coming for global shipping
World.content:
But the novel attacks are also opening a phase of geopolitical crisis where merchant vessels at large are facing the risk of drone attacks. That, in turn, risks causing a maritime arms race.

A remarkable chain of events began in early July: Ukrainian drones started hitting Russian-linked merchant vessels in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov on an almost daily basis. They had struck the occasional shadow vessel in the Mediterranean or Russian oil installations and oil terminals before that, but this campaign was different; several ships were being struck each day.

The culmination was a remarkable 172 ships hit in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov within the course of just 12 days. In fact, Ukraine reported attacks on 15 Russian shadow vessels, including seven tankers and five dry cargo ships, over the course of one night alone.

These attacks then continued, with Ukraine attacking all manner of Russian-linked ships — primarily tankers but others too. In truth, some of the targets have not been shadow vessels, as the illegal fleet primarily operates in the Baltic Sea where ships carrying Russian oil above the price cap traverse to reach their destinations. In the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, far from the Western coastal countries that have imposed the price cap, Russian cargo doesn’t require such workarounds. (These vessels, though, still serve Moscow’s war effort, transporting goods to Crimea and other Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.)

Named MoLoCHKa — a Ukrainian acronym that translates to “Moscow will fall because of Crimea” — the Ukrainian military’s campaign against Russian-linked shipping has been a rude awakening for Moscow, which has had to move drone units from other duties to protect merchant shipping instead.

According to Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces Commander, Robert Brovdi, Moscow has had to deploy up to 200 drone-operator groups to ship-protection duties. It has also begun equipping oil tankers with anti-drone technology, reported the Financial Times.

World.title: New videos show deadly landslide burying gold miners in Central African Republic
World.content:
The footage captures the moment the ground suddenly gives way at the Zamboye artisanal gold mine, engulfing people gathered nearby. Freddy Metchoubatchou was on site when the landslide struck on 18 August and filmed the collapse from close range. The mine is in Nana-Mambéré prefecture, about 50 kilometres from Baboua near the Cameroonian border. Prosecutors in Baboua said several underground tunnels may have collapsed, causing the disaster.

 

Rescue workers were still searching for victims on 21 August, but the number of people underground at the time remains unknown. Recovery efforts have been hampered by limited equipment and expertise.

Local officials, Red Cross volunteers and mining representatives initially reported more than 100 deaths. The Mines Ministry later gave a provisional official toll of 49, including 34 Central African nationals, 13 Cameroonians and two Chadians. Seven injured people were taken to hospital in Baboua.

Authorities have temporarily closed the mine and opened a judicial investigation into the cause of the collapse and possible breaches of mining regulations, including illegal mining and concealed employment.

Artisanal mining is a vital source of income for thousands of people in the Central African Republic, but many sites operate with limited safety equipment, structural reinforcement and emergency-rescue capacity. The disaster follows another deadly mine collapse near the Cameroonian border in June.

World.title: Greece's tourist numbers have risen in 2026, but visitors are spending less
World.content:
Tourism to Greece maintained strong momentum in the first half of 2026, recording a significant increase in both arrivals and travel revenues, according to the latest figures from the Bank of Greece.

 

Between January and June, travel receipts increased by 14.8%, reaching €8.80 billion, while inbound travel traffic rose by 15.4% to 13.49 million travellers.

As a result, the travel balance posted a surplus of €6.93 billion, compared with €6.01 billion in the same period of 2025.

The picture in June

In June 2026, travel receipts came to €3.48 billion, marking a relatively modest year-on-year increase of 1.2%. At the same time, arrivals grew much more strongly, by 6.9%, reaching 4.92 million travellers.

This divergence is mainly explained by a 6.2% drop in average spending per trip, indicating that the rise in visitor numbers did not translate into a similar increase in revenues.

Inbound travel traffic recorded robust growth in the first half, with arrivals from EU-27 countries up by 19.3%. Particularly striking was the increase in traffic through road border crossings, up by 49.3%, while arrivals via airports rose by 7.3%.

Among the key markets, arrivals from Germany increased by 10.4%, from Italy by 17.9% and from the United Kingdom by 10.4%.

file photo AP Photo/Yorgos Karahalis

Travel receipts by country of origin

At the level of individual markets, the picture for travel receipts in the first half of 2026 shows marked differences.

Overall, receipts from residents of the EU-27 increased by 10.7%, reaching €4.53 billion, while the rise in receipts from other countries was even stronger, at 19.7%, to €3.86 billion.

Within the EU, euro area countries generated €3.78 billion, up 13.3%, while receipts from non-euro area EU countries fell by 1.1%.

Germany

Germany remained one of the most important markets for Greek tourism, with receipts of €1.276 billion in the first half. However, this amount was 6.3% lower than in the same period of 2025.

It is noteworthy that arrivals from Germany increased by 10.4%, to 2.04 million travellers. In other words, more Germans visited Greece, without this being reflected in higher overall revenues.

The trend became particularly evident in June, when receipts from Germany fell by 14.5%, to €515.1 million, even though arrivals rose by 6.0%.

France

The French market also moved in a negative direction. Receipts from France in the first half fell by 7.4%, to €414.3 million, while arrivals remained virtually unchanged, edging down by 0.4%.

The decline was much sharper in June: receipts dropped by 33.9%, to €129.8 million, while arrivals of French travellers were down by 18.5%. France is therefore one of the key markets that weighed on revenues in that particular month.

Italy

At the other end of the spectrum, Italy posted a particularly strong performance. Receipts in the first half increased by 31.1%, reaching €470.0 million, while arrivals were up by 17.9%.

The positive trend strengthened in June, when receipts from Italian travellers rose by 34.4%, to €248.3 million, with arrivals also recording a significant increase of 21.8%.

Italy is thus among the markets making the strongest positive contribution to the rise in tourism revenues.

file photo AP Photo/Thanassis Stavrakis

United Kingdom

The United Kingdom was also a key source of tourism revenues. In the first half, receipts reached €1.179 billion, an increase of 8.5%, while arrivals rose by 10.4% to 1.68 million travellers.

However, the picture in June was quite different: receipts fell by 26.1%, to €442.9 million, and arrivals declined by 12.0%. So, despite the positive overall performance in the half-year, June saw a marked slowdown in the British market.

United States

The overall contribution of the United States was also positive. Receipts from American travellers increased by 10.8% in the first half, reaching €796.9 million.

This development is particularly noteworthy because arrivals from the US decreased by 5.4%, to 656.7 thousand travellers.

This suggests that, unlike other markets, total revenues from the US rose despite the drop in visitor numbers.

In June, however, receipts decreased by 3.7%, to €257.8 million, while arrivals fell by 12.1%.

Note from the Bank of Greece: Inbound travel traffic does not include data from cruises, other than those recorded by the Border Survey.

World.title: Dubai’s competitive advantage for digital business
World.content:
‘Partner Content’ is used to describe brand content that is paid for and controlled by the advertiser rather than the Euronews editorial team. This content is produced by commercial departments and does not involve Euronews editorial staff or news journalists. The funding partner has control of the topics, content and final approval in collaboration with Euronews’ commercial production department.

Dubai is building a digital economy designed to attract the next generation of high-growth companies.

 

Advanced infrastructure, forward-looking regulation and global connectivity are helping the emirate strengthen its position as a hub for digital business, while a growing ecosystem gives startups access to investors, partners and opportunities to scale.

And the numbers show the momentum behind that ambition.

A hub built for the digital age

Dubai’s business environment is geared towards digital companies looking to establish themselves, develop new products and expand into international markets. More than 20 free zones, alongside a network of incubators and accelerators, provide support for startups and scaleups at different stages of growth.

These dedicated zones allow entities to operate with specialised framework advantages while remaining seamlessly integrated into the city's overarching technological landscape.

Dubai Chamber of Digital Economy is also building connections across the ecosystem through a series of initiatives that address key friction points that early-stage and expanding businesses typically encounter, ranging from market entry logistics to talent acquisition and venture capital access.

The chamber’s Business in Dubai initiative helps companies enter the market and link with potential partners, investors and customers. It serves as a soft-landing mechanism, helping founders navigate regulatory processes and build immediate commercial pipelines.

Meanwhile, Dubai Founders HQ, a joint initiative between Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism (DET) and Dubai Chamber of Digital Economy, provides a dedicated platform for founders, investors, corporates and ecosystem partners to collaborate, exchange knowledge and structure strategic partnerships under one unified umbrella.

The numbers behind the growth

Dubai’s Information and Communication sector contributed €11.1 billion (AED 12.1 billion) to the emirate’s GDP in Q1 2026, growing 2.7% year-on-year and accounting for 5.2% of total GDP.

Digital transformation is also central to the Dubai Economic Agenda (D33), which targets €24.8 billion (US$27 billion) in annual economic value from digital transformation projects. This strategic agenda underscores the government's commitment to embedding technology across all sectors of the economy, ensuring sustained long-term growth.

That ambition is already extending beyond generative AI. In May 2026, Dubai launched a two-year initiative to accelerate the adoption of Agentic AI across the private sector, supported by specialised training, incubators and dedicated funding. By moving early to support the commercial use of autonomous AI systems, the emirate is positioning its business ecosystem for the next wave of technological change.

This wider digital push is also being reflected in the growth of Dubai’s startup community. During 2025, Dubai Chamber of Digital Economy supported 1,690 digital startups in establishing or expanding their presence in Dubai, an increase of 39.7% compared with 2024. International companies accounted for 75% of those supported, while AI-focused companies represented around 15% and fintech companies 12%.

Dubai is also home to Expand North Star, an annual event that brings startups together with investors and potential business partners. It has become a major meeting point for founders and investors, giving startups access to capital and new markets while bringing global technology companies into Dubai’s wider digital economy ecosystem.

Expand North Star’s 10th edition, held in October 2025, brought together more than 2,000 startups and 1,200 investors managing €1.01 trillion (US$1.1 trillion) in assets. It also featured 40 unicorns with a combined valuation of €828 billion (US$900 billion).

Together, these figures demonstrate that Dubai’s digital expansion is not just hypothetical - it is backed by measurable economic output, ambitious government targets and a rapidly surging intake of foreign tech ventures.

Regulatory clarity as a competitive edge

For companies working in developing sectors, regulation is increasingly part of the infrastructure they need to grow.

Clear and predictable legal frameworks reduce regulatory uncertainty, enabling founders and investors to make long-term commitments with confidence.

Dubai’s Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA) oversees virtual assets and virtual asset activities across Dubai, excluding the Dubai International Financial Centre. Its regulatory structure sets out requirements for companies operating in the sector and provides a defined framework for virtual asset activities.

For Dubai Chamber of Digital Economy, the wider goal is to create an environment in which digital companies can establish themselves and scale internationally.

Saeed Al Gergawi, Vice President of Dubai Chamber of Digital Economy, commented: “Dubai’s approach is focused on creating the right conditions for digital companies to innovate, grow and scale with confidence. This means developing a business environment that combines regulatory clarity with the flexibility needed to keep pace with rapidly evolving technologies, while connecting companies with the talent, capital and partnerships they need to succeed globally.”

By turning ambitious vision into measurable momentum, Dubai has built far more than a business hub - it has created a place where global founders can transform bold ideas into world-changing scale.

World.title: French driver discovers 1.5 metre boa constrictor under car bonnet
World.content:
The boa constrictor, which can grow to more than 3 metres in length, actually lives in South America, where it is found from Colombia to Argentina.

 

So a motorist in Colomiers, a suburb of Toulouse in France, got quite a shock when he discovered a 1.5-metre-long snake of this species under his car bonnet. The discovery was made when the driver was about to change the battery of the car, which had not been driven for a month, according to the Haute-Garonne fire brigade's Facebook page.

Five firefighters, two of them from the RAN (Animal rescue firefighter) specialist unit for incidents involving animals, managed to carefully transfer the boa from the car's engine compartment into a glass container.

The fire brigade also shared the operation on social media in an effort to find out where the constrictor came from. The animal was handed over to a local veterinary school.

Boa constrictors like warm conditions. France's successive recent heatwaves are therefore likely to have made it easier for escaped exotic boas to survive in the wild.

Rescue services also stress that keeping snakes in France is subject to strict rules that must be followed.

A few days after the car bonnet boa incident, animal experts from the Toulouse fire brigade were called out to Montesquieu-Volvestre, where another 1-metre-long boa had escaped from a vivarium.

Is the boa constrictor dangerous to humans?

A few years ago an American woman had to call the emergency services after her pet boa constrictor latched on to her face.

Normally, boas, which feed mainly on insects, spiders and smaller animals such as lizards, do not pose a danger to adult humans. This species of snake has no venomous fangs. A bite can be painful, but above all the boa constrictor, as its name suggests, kills its prey by swiftly coiling its body around it and constricting it to death.

Constrictor snakes are among the protected vertebrates and fall under the Washington CITES agreement (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora). In addition, the European Union has further legal provisions that must be complied with when buying, keeping and breeding boas.

World.title: Syrians who came home after al-Assad's fall find a complicated reality
World.content:
Nearly two years after Bashar al-Assad's ouster, the Syrians who rushed to go back home are discovering that what they left behind is no longer what they remember — and that coming home to a country fresh out of war comes with its own challenges.

 

"I regret coming back," Samer told Euronews. "In Turkey I was making about $1,000. Today my income doesn't surpass $250-300."

Samer* returned from Turkey after the fall of al-Assad's regime. His colleague Mustafa returned from Egypt at the same time. Working side by side in the same Damascus barbershop, they have reached opposite conclusions about whether they made the right choice.

Mustafa lives in his family home and pays no rent. He is back working for the barber who trained him. There he earns around $300 a month, or roughly twice what remained after Cairo rent ate into his Egyptian wages. He does not regret coming back.

Samer does. "My dream is to be able to buy a motorbike for $400, and I still can't, just so I can save on transport fares," he said.

"I ran into a harsh reality. Barbershops here do not offer the services I used to provide, and the wages are so low they do not even cover the cost of getting from my home in Maraba, in rural Damascus, to the Mezzeh district in the heart of the capital, a distance of around 20 km," he explained.

"My whole life has changed: the cost of living is high, infrastructure is weak and there are constant power cuts, and electricity is essential to the work of a barber."

The end of al-Assad's rule in December 2024 prompted one of the fastest mass returns of refugees and displaced people in recent history.

By the end of May 2026, UNHCR counted roughly 1.67 million Syrians who had returned from neighbouring countries, alongside 1.92 million internally displaced people who had gone back to their areas of origin.

That adds up to nearly 3.6 million people mostly in Aleppo, Idlib, rural areas near Damascus and the capital itself.

Syrians returning from displacement in Lebanon take a "selfie" as soon as they arrive at the Jdeidat Yabous border crossing with Syria, Tuesday 29 July 2025. AP Photo

They all returned to a country the World Bank estimates has sustained $108 billion in direct physical damage, with reconstruction needs of around $216 billion — or roughly 10 times Syria's entire GDP in 2024.

Homes remain damaged or destroyed, power cuts are frequent, civil administration is dysfunctional and formal employment is scarce.

Caught between two worlds

Mawia al-Shaer came back from Germany with her three children, the eldest 10, the youngest six. All had studied in German, but they are now in Arabic-language schools following a curriculum they have never come across before.

"There is a big difference between schooling in Syria and in Germany," al-Shaer told Euronews. "Private schools are extremely expensive here, whereas in Germany the service was free."

Private schools in Damascus charge at least $2,000 per child per year. State schools are overcrowded. Al-Shaer cannot afford the first and does not trust the second.

"This will make my children feel withdrawn and afraid and unwilling to go to school," she said.

"Everything will change for them: the overcrowded classrooms, their inability to express themselves, which may expose them to bullying or class prejudice because of the different language and way of thinking they acquired in Germany," al-Shaer added.

She now wishes she had visited her relatives and returned to Germany before the new school year began.

Syrian refugee Anas Modamani (27) displays his famous "selfie" with Merkel inside a restaurant in Berlin, 10 December 2024. AP Photo

Amer Hassan arrived from Germany with more than $45,000 in savings. He wanted to open a restaurant. He paid rent, started fitting out the space and ran out of money before it opened.

"I got roughly halfway and then it all came to a halt," Hassan told Euronews. "I couldn't complete what I had dreamed of."

"If I had been in Germany, I would have received government support in the form of loans, and with half the money I spent I could have launched the business," he added.

"Rents are extremely, extremely high, and labour costs are also high. I've gone back to square one."

He holds German citizenship and he said he plans to go back.

"I will return and try to start over there," Hassan explained. "Here I have run out of options and lost what I had built up during my stay and asylum in Europe."

Fares Ibrahim and his wife Lida returned from Sweden and opened a tailoring shop in Damascus's Shaalan district.

They put $10,000 into rent and $5,000 into equipment. Six months later, they had made less than $1,000 in profit, so they were forced to close the shop.

"We are now looking for premises in a rural area where the rent is lower, so we can get back on our feet," Ibrahim told Euronews.

The wall of bureaucracy

Munir is a teacher who came back from Jordan. He has spent months trying to secure a position through Syria's education ministry, but nothing has come through.

"Every month I knock on the doors of the ministry or the education directorate to see whether my appointment has gone through, but in vain," Munir told Euronews.

"There is never a response, every time there's a different excuse." He has stopped waiting and taken up farming.

"I have now stopped teaching and am working the land, doing farming and sowing seeds just to get by," he explained.

"I have set aside my experience and years of study in Jordan, and I wish I could work in Syria instead of having to think about travelling in search of a teaching post in good schools that also pay decent salaries."

Syrians wait to cross from Turkey to Syria at the Oncupinar border crossing, near the town of Kilis in southern Turkey, Thursday 12 December 2024. AP Photo

Said Mahrouz returned from Sweden with a master's degree in computer engineering. The first eight months, he said, "were hell".

He sold his mother's jewellery to raise capital, spent months on licences and paperwork, and at one point considered going back.

Today he runs a small programming and networking company. "The Syrian market needs a lot, but you have to understand it first," he said.

"The business began to stabilise, and now I only consider travelling to attend international fairs that can help develop my company."

Kamal Kikhiya has lived in Germany for 15 years. He spoke to friends and relatives who went back. He has decided not to join them.

"They all feel regret. Some returned to destroyed villages, others couldn't even manage to open a small supermarket," Kikhiya told Euronews.

He has a six-year-old son in German school. "I cannot gamble with my family's future in a country whose future is still so uncertain."

*Euronews has used first names or pseudonyms for Samer, Mustafa and Munir at their request, to protect their privacy and personal safety.

World.title: Sweden plans to send migrants to Italy, France and Spain reject Dublin transfers
World.content:
More and more European governments are announcing their intention to transfer, or that they have already transferred, so-called Dublin transferees to Italy.

 

After Germany, Switzerland, Austria and Finland, Sweden has also confirmed to Italian news agency ANSA that it intends to "apply the rules as set out" in the new EU Pact on Asylum and Migration, which entered into force on 12 June, and that it expects "all member states to fulfil their obligations," Italy included.

Spain and France are taking the opposite line, two other countries that are key points of first entry into Europe for migrants, and have distanced themselves from sending migrants back to the country of first entry.

However, the issue of the suspension of Schengen, introduced due to the migration crisis in Ceuta and remaining in force until 31 August, is still unresolved with Madrid.

Who the Dublin transferees are and how many there are

Dublin transferees are people who have arrived in Europe to seek asylum and who, under the Dublin Regulation and the new EU Pact on Migration, are required to lodge their asylum application in the first country they enter.

According to Eurostat, from 2023 to 2025, Rome received 109,427 transfer requests (2023 (source in Italian); 2024 (source in Italian); 2025 (source in Italian)).

Taking the 2025 data as an example, Italy is by far the country that has received the highest number of transfer requests for Dublin transferees, over 24,000, according to Eurostat.

Of these, 14,000, the largest share, come from Germany and France and would therefore be cancelled thanks to an agreement signed by Interior Minister Piantedosi (source in Italian) with the European Union's Justice and Home Affairs Council at the end of 2025.

But a further 10,000 remain pending, and the main countries of origin of these requests are precisely those now making themselves heard: Switzerland (3,612 requests), Austria (644), Finland (520), Belgium (1,531), and a few hundred more spread across other countries, starting with Sweden.

Austria, in particular, has told LaPresse that since the Pact came into force, it has already returned four Dublin transferees to Italy.

Italy received the largest number of incoming requests (24,152, Eurostat estimate) Eurostat

How Italy is blocking the transfer of Dublin transferees

Italy, however, unilaterally halted transfers at the end of 2022, despite a 2024 ruling (source in Italian) to the contrary, which holds that Rome cannot, in substance, evade its Dublin obligations, since it is assumed that an EU member state is capable of guaranteeing dignified reception conditions for asylum seekers.

And in an initial assessment (source in Italian) of the new EU Pact on Asylum and Migration, the Commission notes that Italy is still refusing transfers: between 12 June and 7 July, it is reported to have already rejected 12.

With specific reference to the Italian case, the text in fact states that "a receiving member state cannot refuse a transfer and (...) must propose an alternative date for the transfer".

Time limits for lodging and examining asylum applications

Under the Dublin Regulation before the new Pact, after 12 months, if the transfer to the first country of arrival has not taken place, the asylum seeker is freed from that obligation and can apply in the country where they are actually present.

It should be stressed, however, that the new European Pact on Migration extends the responsibility of the country of first arrival for the asylum application to 20 months.

Moreover, from its entry into force, the vast majority of asylum seekers should know the outcome of their application within 12 weeks.

But less than three months have passed since the new Pact entered into force and, as Piantedosi explained to the Schengen Committee last week, it is therefore still too early to draw up a balance sheet.

It is nonetheless legitimate to ask whether a country such as Italy will be able to repatriate migrants from safe countries who are denied asylum within just three months.

A first, partial answer will come with the next monitoring exercise by the European Commission, scheduled for mid-October.

Why do France and Spain choose not to join the countries sending Dublin transferees back to Italy?

Given the current state of play on migration, it is understandable that many European countries have started to raise their voices with Italy, particularly after the move to suspend Schengen with Spain and Meloni's stance, completely at odds with the solidarity required under the new Pact, on tackling irregular migration.

Unlike the Nordic countries, France has for now decided "not to join the countries" that are sending migrants back to Italy, well-informed sources in Paris told ANSA, at least "for as long as this phase of cooperation and rapprochement" with Rome continues. The two countries, the sources explain, "share the wish to work to bring down the flows departing from Tunisia and Libya".

The Spanish government is likewise "in favour" of handling the issue of the so-called Dublin transferees through the European solidarity mechanisms provided for in the European Pact on Migration and Asylum and in the European Union's recent legislation, "rather than resorting to isolated bilateral expulsions or restrictions", sources at Spain's Interior Ministry also told ANSA.

Political reactions in Italy to the Dublin transferees crisis

The affair is inevitably fuelling political controversy in Italy, which had already erupted after the Ceuta crisis and the Schengen row with Spain, and which Elly Schlein sees as "a spectacular boomerang from Giorgia Meloni's propaganda stunt".

"Because of her blind ideology, she has never pursued the most important battle to be fought in Brussels in the national interest: that for European solidarity, including on reception", said the leader of the main opposition party.

Giuseppe Conte was sarcastic about the prime minister's "masterpiece": "Repatriations are working, but against us," he wrote on social media.

"There is no link between the suspension of Schengen over the events in Ceuta and the legitimate choice by some European countries to restart the relocations of Dublin transferees," explained Carlo Fidanza, head of the Brothers of Italy delegation in the European Parliament, arguing that "the issue concerns only a small number of cases between August 2025 and 11 June 2026" and that "for those who entered after 12 June, the number of potential relocations will fall sharply".

World.title: Could magnesium become the new lithium for electric vehicles?
World.content:
In the last few years, lithium has emerged as one of the most crucial metals for the global electric transition.

 

This is mainly due to its widespread usage in electric vehicles (EVs), through lithium-ion batteries. These provide high energy density, a lightweight structure and fast-charging capacity, along with a long cycle life, which supports modern driving range and performance.

As such, it has become key to achieving widespread, practical advancements in automotive electrification.

However, lithium continues to face vital long-term structural supply challenges, which has led to more EV producers considering other alternatives like manganese and magnesium.

Why magnesium?

Magnesium, another critical metal for electric vehicles and energy storage batteries, could potentially be a key alternative to lithium in EVs.

This is because it is cheaper, abundantly found across the world and also stores more energy. It is also considered to be safer than lithium, as it does not form the sharp spikes known as dendrites that cause lithium batteries to sometimes short or catch fire.

A magnesium battery can also hold more energy in a smaller space, which could have significant size and efficiency benefits for EV makers who want to make more compact vehicles.

It is also one of the most common elements found both in seawater and in the ground, which could help makers bypass potential supply constraints with lithium down the line.

Magnesium ions also carry double the charge of lithium ions, at a +2 charge, which can help support a higher volumetric capacity, enabling more compact, energy-dense power storage for both EVs and other devices.

China produces the overwhelming majority of the world's magnesium, accounting for around 87% to 95% of the world's primary magnesium in 2025, coming up to anywhere between 830,000 and 950,000 metric tons, according to Visual Capitalist's Elements.

This is mainly from extensive dolomite reserves, with the largest magnesium reserves being in the Liaoning province.

The second top producer of magnesium is Israel, which extracts the metal mainly from the Dead Sea. Russia and Brazil are other major producers, with some key magnesium reserves being located in Satka and Brumado.

Manganese is also emerging as a support to lithium batteries, rather than fully replacing them. This is due to manganese batteries having a much lower energy density and not being easily rechargeable hundreds of times. They also provide lower voltage.

As such, they work well to support lithium systems in hybrid setups but fail under heavy power demands.

Why lithium supplies are fickle

One of the biggest challenges facing lithium supply is slow project timelines. This is because opening a new lithium mine takes an average of 16 to 18 years, from initial discovery to first production. This is mainly due to complex permitting rules, exploration rights and financing issues in many regions of the world.

Hard rock mining also produces significant waste and brine extraction consumes vast amounts of water in the arid regions lithium is usually found in. This leads to more scrutiny from local communities and environmental groups as well.

Similarly, due to lithium prices having crashed recently, following previous oversupply, mining investment and exploration budgets have now reduced somewhat. This significantly threatens the pipeline for future production and the global green transition.

The majority of lithium is also concentrated in Australia and South America’s “Lithium Triangle,” whereas China controls a significant portion of the refining capacity required to make battery-grade material.

Magnesium batteries?

Currently, most magnesium batteries still in the testing phase by entities like the University of Waterloo.

However, some major automakers are increasingly developing and experimenting with magnesium-rich or manganese-doped alternatives like Lithium Manganese-Rich or LMFP cells or long-term magnesium chemistry.

MG (SAIC Motor) has recently deployed new Lithium-Manganese-Oxide (LMO) semi-solid-state SolidCore battery tech in models like the MG4 EV Urban, which is scheduled to hit UK and European markets by the end of 2026.

General Motors and LG Energy Solution are currently aiming for a 2028 commerical launch for advanced lithium manganese-rich (LMR) battery cells. These use high manganese content to decrease costs and raise energy density for future electric trucks and SUVs.

Similarly, Toyota has also funded long-term dedicated research into replacing standard lithium chemistry with high-capacity magnesium alternatives. However, it is still unclear when commercial vehicles could be using this technology, as researchers are still awaiting further electrolyte stabilisation.

Great Wall Motor also uses semi-solid magnesium casting technology to reduce component weight, while Tesla integrated selective magnesium alloy components inot the Model 3 and Model Y.

Why magnesium batteries are not as widespread yet

While magnesium batteries are seeing more interest as potential alternatives to lithium now, significant challenges remain before they can be mass-adopted yet.

One of the biggest drawbacks of magnesium is slow ion movement, which means that magnesium particles move more slowly inside the battery materials.

This causes very slow charging times and weak power during fast acceleration, along with poor cold-weather performance. These factors could make it much harder for magnesium batteries to match fast-charging and high-power lithium EV batteries.

Finding a liquid, solid or electrolyte that lets magnesium move easily without breaking down is hard too, currently, as electrolytes that successfully move magnesium ions efficiently end up corroding the internal battery components.

Similarly, finding a cathode material that can withstand insertion and removal of magnesium ions without breaking down remains incredibly complex.

World.title: What to do when wildfires trigger trauma
World.content:
The wildfires this summer have broken records in Germany and are unlikely to subside in future. Psychologists say post-traumatic stress disorder caused by such disasters is serious but can be treated if people seek help.

This year, wildfires have already burned more land than the annual average from 2006 to 2025 in Germany. North Rhine-Westphalia, the country's most populous state, has just seen the largest recorded wildfire in its history. It destroyed or damaged about 300 to 400 hectares in the Hürtgen Forest in the Eifel region.

After weeks without rain, the wildfire spread rapidly across the arid landscape with wind driving the flames in different directions. Unexploded munitions from World War II that were at risk of exploding or did explode complicated the firefighting efforts. Around 1,500 firefighters battled the flames for almost a week until the fire was stabilized, with some working 12-hour shifts.

Peter Berndgen, a spokesperson for the volunteer fire department in the Düren district in the west of the state, said that the physical and mental strain was enormous.

"My eyes itch every night, my nose is always black, and my airways and lungs are under pressure. During a 12-hour-shift, you're constantly on high alert, ready for whatever might happen," he said. This can be trees falling or the flames changing direction, he added.

And on top of that, the constant fear that "the situation is spiraling out of my control, we won't be able to cope, you get that kind of feeling sometimes. And then you start wondering whether you'll manage to get it under control at all."

Can Germany teach Europe how to prevent wildfires? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Not everyone suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder

Despite being prepared and professional, firefighters know they are also at risk of death. "The fear, or dread, that you can have is really, where can I take refuge, how will I get out of this. I'm right in the middle of a forest."

Andreas Meyer, a psychiatrist from the Central Institute of Mental Health in Mannheim who co-authored the "Berlin Declaration on Climate Change and Mental Health," says such situations can have long-lasting effects.

"Not everyone, but several people who experience something like this end up developing what is known as post-traumatic stress disorder. They find themselves reliving the event over and over, having nightmares, and experiencing flashbacks. Post-traumatic stress disorder is three times more common among firefighters than it is in the general population."

A typical symptom of post-traumatic stress disorder is avoidance behavior. People might avoid places that resemble those where the trauma first occurred, as well as conversations about the event itself.

"This can lead to the disorder setting in," said Meyer-Lindenberg.

He explained that it was totally normal to feel shaken immediately after such a disaster; to have trouble sleeping, for example, or to feel sad, but he said that if such a state persisted for more than a month and interfered with daily life, people should seek psychological help.

"The good news is that post-traumatic stress disorder can be treated very successfully with behavioral therapy," he said, adding that it resolved the disorder in two-thirds of patients.

Apart from post-traumatic stress disorder, wildfires and other such disasters can also trigger depression, anxiety disorder or addiction. Some studies have found that people are also more likely to self-harm or even commit suicide afterward.

Meyer-Lindenberg said that the number of psychiatric diagnoses is likely to double after such a disaster. "Fortunately, for many of those affected, the symptoms subside on their own. But, unfortunately, this is not always the case. Illness might still be detected years later."

'A new normal': Unprecedented wildfires in Canada To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Some population groups more likely to be affected, particularly women

Some groups of the population are more likely to be affected than others, studies have found. For example, children and adolescents, as well as people who are poor or who already had a mental illness. Women are also more likely to be affected than men.

While one in three people affected by a natural disaster is at risk of developing long-lasting post-traumatic stress disorder, this falls to one in 10 amid emergency responders.

Meyer-Lindenberg said that they were helped by experience, clear rules during an operation and working together as a team.

"So much depends on these factors when you are confronted with an emergency," he said. "Do I feel capable? Do I know what I have to do? Do I have colleagues, teammates I can rely on? Is there a structure in place or am I at the mercy of a situation?"

While ordinary people might be forced to stand by as their neighborhood goes up in flames, firefighters have the task of putting out the fire.

Peter Berndgen said that the volunteer firefighters in the Rhine region were highly motivated. "We want to protect ourselves, the population, our villages, our homes. We want to protect all of that," he said. "And I believe that gives us energy."

He added that psychological support was on hand if necessary and that talking about experiences was a routine part of operations as well as fighting the flames.

Taking action and control can be useful in fighting feeling of helplessness

Meyer-Lindenberg said that everyone affected by a natural disaster could benefit from action and taking control of their situation if possible. He said it was useful to put in place preventative measures against fires or floods, for example. However, it was not helpful to try to toughen oneself up for a disaster or to get used to them.

"Quite the contrary: if someone has already lived through such a disaster, they are more likely to suffer psychological consequences from the next one," he said

Firefighters who are able to put out a fire, as Berndgen and his colleagues did in the Hürtgen Forest, are also less likely to suffer from long-term psychological stress. "It confirms that what we did made sense," he said.

Unfortunately, he did not feel the same during the flood in the Ahr Valley five years ago, he said. "People from the Ahr region whose lives were in danger called us for help, but we knew we couldn't help them."

That is the worst possible situation for a firefighter, he said. "If I knew that I'd have to do this every six months, I would probably reach a point and ask whether I could really cope."

This article was originally published in German

World.title: Sweden: Several wounded in school sword attack
World.content:
Police say they have arrested an individual who stabbed several people with a sword at a high school in central Sweden.

A person armed with a sword has wounded multiple people at a school in Fagersta in central Sweden, authorities said Friday.

"Police have responded to the scene and one person ​has been taken into custody," a police statement said.

Authorities did not specify how many people were injured in the attack.

"Police are ​continuing to work at ​the scene ‌with a number of different resources. The ​public ⁠is urged to respect the roadblocks ⁠and ​listen to police instructions," the police statement said.

Other schools locked down

The municipality said police were searching the school premesis and that other schools in the area had been locked down.

Meanwhile, public broadcaster SVT reported that ambulances, police cars and a police helicopter were outside the school.

Justice Minister Gunnar Strommer told Reuters news agency the government was in close contact with the police ​following the attack.

"We ​have been ⁠informed of a serious incident in Fagersta. The ⁠police ​are on site and working very intensively with the incident," Strommer said.

More to come...

World.title: Swiss tourist jailed in Bali for insulting Hindu holiday
World.content:
The 26-year-old was given a one-year prison sentence for offensive remarks posted on Instagram. During the trial, he apologized to the Balinese people for denigrating the Day of Silence and said he regretted his actions.

A Swiss man has been sentenced to one year in prison on the Indonesian resort island of Bali after insulting a sacred Hindu holiday.

A judge in the city of Denpasar found the 26-year-old guilty of making derogatory remarks on social media about the traditional "Nyepi," or Day of Silence.

On that day each year, people on the predominantly Hindu island are required to stay home and forgo work, the internet and entertainment. Streets and beaches are empty, except for special patrols tasked with ensuring that silence is observed. Even the international airport is shut down.

According to the public prosecutor's office, the Swiss tourist was informed about the Day of Silence rules by hotel staff when he arrived in Bali in February.

The 26-year-old arrived in Bali in February and has been kept in pre-trial detention since his arrest in March Image: Ni Komang Erviani/AFP

In video clips posted to Instagram, he boasted that he had defied the restrictions and walked to a beach during the observance. He also ranted against the tradition, calling it "crazy" and using an expletive.

The man was arrested in March after the videos sparked widespread anger and complaints to police.

"What the defendant did offended the Balinese people, hurt their faith and provoked public outrage," said presiding judge Tjokorda Putra Budi Pastima. "The defendant must be held accountable for his actions."

Digital nomads in Bali: Working from Paradise To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Man apologizes, saying he was hungry

During the trial in June, the defendant told the court he did not understand the extent of the restrictions and that it was not his intention to insult the Balinese people or their holiday.

He said he made the Instagram posts while hungry and frustrated that he could not find food during the holy day.

"I deeply regret what I did. I apologize to the Balinese people," the man said.

Since his arrest, the 26-year-old has spent five months in pre-trial detention — time that will be deducted from his one-year prison term.

Authorities in Switzerland said they were providing him with consular assistance.

World.title: Germany investigates arms cache found in woods near Berlin
World.content:
Handguns and ammunition were found in a forest near Berlin last year. German authorities suspect they were to be used for assassinations on behalf of Russian intelligence.

Security authorities in Germany uncovered a cache of handguns in a forest near the capital Berlin last year, which they believe was intended to be used to carry out assassinations on behalf of Russia, according to reports on Friday.

The daily Süddeutsche Zeitung and public broadcasters NDR and WDR reported that one suspect was arrested in Romania.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said German authorities were in touch with their Romanian counterparts about the suspect's potential extradition.

"This case demonstrates that we are ​operating under a high threat level," ​Dobrindt told a press ​conference.

What else did Dobrindt say about the weapons stash?

Dobrindt confirmed the media reports that the suspect, who was detained in Romania last year, was being investigated on suspicion of espionage and planning a violent attack that endangers the state.

But Dobrindt did not comment on the media reports' claims that the weapons were meant to be used for targeted killings on behalf of Russian intelligence. The minister only said that authorities could not rule out foreign powers being involved.

The interior minister also did not disclose the suspect's identity, but he did say that the suspect was being held in connection with planned parcel bomb attacks in Romania.

"We will then determine, in the course of the investigation, what measures ​can be ⁠taken against this person," Dobrindt added.

Dobrindt said the suspect was a "low-level agent" and unaware of the line of command above him. The minister added that other operatives, including a Kazakh citizen, had been detained this year who were similarly uninformed of the network they were part of.

Interior Minister Dobrindt refused to confirm reports that Russia was involved in the arms cache Image: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

What do we know about the weapons that were found?

The stash found near Berlin contained two pistols, which had signs that they had been placed there on behalf of Russia's intelligence services, German news agency dpa reported. The stash also contained ammunition.

Police disabled the two handguns but left them intact at the site before placing the location under surveillance.

Dobrindt said officers watched the stash for months after discovering it, but no one was seen approaching it. It is presumed the alleged perpetrators were aware that police had uncovered the weapons and avoided the site.

What do we know about Russia's alleged involvement?

While Dobrindt refused to be drawn into whether Russia was directly involved, the minister said this month that Germany was a "daily target of hybrid warfare."

"Espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, or covert operations by foreign powers aimed at destabilizing Germany or inflicting direct harm are a constant reality," Dobrindt said at the time.

Those remarks came in response to the discovery of an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig Airport.

Some German lawmakers have pointed to Russia, and US media reports said American intelligence services suspected that Russia was behind the drone incident.

Russia has rejected allegations that it was involved as a ⁠"hastily fabricated provocation" that is part of a "new wave of anti-Russian hysteria in Germany."

The Russian embassy in Berlin added that the incident "only serves the interests of Kyiv and the militarist wing of the European political class."

World.title: Ceuta: Spanish police arrest 5 alleged migrant traffickers
World.content:
The arrests come after Spain's North African exclave saw a deadly border surge in late July, when tens of thousands of migrants entered Ceuta.

Spanish police have arrested five people suspected of charging migrants thousands of euros to bring them from Ceuta, Spain's North African exclave, to mainland Spain.

The arrests come less than a month after the Spanish territory, which borders Morocco, saw a deadly border rush in which over 70,000 migrants entered Ceuta irregularly, with many swimming or crossing on foot.

Dozens of people died in the chaotic scenes. Ceuta's leader Juan Jesus Vivas told EU lawmakers that some 100 people had died, while Spanish NGO Caminando Fronteras said the death toll was 141 people.

The incident renewed debate in Europe on the sensitive issue of migration. Italy temporarily suspended Schengen border-free travel with Spain in response, with Madrid retaliating by imposing border controls on travelers from Italy.

Spain's Ceuta grapples with aftermath of border chaos To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did Spanish police say about the arrests?

Five people were arrested after two investigations in Ceuta and in La Linea de la Concepcion in Andalusia, which borders British overseas territory Gibraltar.

The suspected traffickers allegedly charged migrants up to €9,000 ($10,500), Spain's Interior Ministry said in a statement , adding that the suspects used small boats "to smuggle migrants from Ceuta to the mainland."

Four of the people arrested are alleged members of a trafficking network that picked up undocumented migrants, sheltered them in houses or garages in Ceuta before smuggling them across the Strait of Gibraltar to Spain.

"Boat drivers were selected for their experience navigating fast and their ability to make evasive manoeuvres and avoid police checks," the statement said.

In one of the crossings, seven people were crammed into an overcrowded dinghy that was barely five meters (16 feet) long and two meters wide for five hours, without life jackets or other adequate safety equipment, police said. The boat ran out of fuel and was left adrift in the Strait of Gibraltar.

Strong currents, changing tides, high winds and heavy maritime traffic combine to make the Strait of Gibraltar extremely dangerous for people attempting to cross it in small boats.

What is the current situation in Ceuta?

Most of the estimated 72,000 migrants who entered Ceuta in late July have returned to Morocco, Spanish officials say. But thousands remain in the enclave, sleeping in makeshift camps, on the street or on the beach.

More than 1,000 migrants were cleared from Trampolin Beach on Friday, after more than 1,200 people were evacuated from the site the day before and moved to shelters.

The Spanish government in Madrid has said it will open temporary centers to ease the burden on Ceuta's overcrowded migrant shelters.

World.title: DRC Ebola outbreak 'growing exponentially,' UN says
World.content:
The Ebola outbreak in the DRC is rapidly spreading in an area "bigger than France," according to a senior UN official. The WHO is providing the country with thousands of vaccine doses in a bid to contain the virus.

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is "growing exponentially" and risks spilling over into neighboring countries unless containment efforts are stepped up, the UN's senior Ebola coordinator said Friday.

The outbreak is already the deadliest in the country's history, with more than 2,500 deaths from over 5,000 infections.

"The epidemic is spreading widely. It's now covering an area that is bigger than France," UN senior Ebola coordinator Julien Harneis told journalists, adding that half of the 2,500 deaths had been reported in the last 20 days alone.

"It is growing faster and wider than the Ebola response."

He stressed that aid funding and the delivery of resources to remote areas needed to be urgently ramped up to slow and eventually stop the virus's transmission.

"If we do not ... then this epidemic will become more deadly. It will spread wider and it risks to spread into neighboring countries," Harneis added.

Ebola outbreak in DR Congo outpaces efforts to contain it To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak in history

The current epidemic is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare type of Ebola that has no approved vaccine or treatment.

The first infections were detected earlier this year in the DRC's northeastern Ituri province, an area where armed groups operate and health infrastructure is poor. The virus has since spread to five other provinces as well as to neighboring Uganda.

Medical workers carry out disinfection work to prevent further infections at an Ebola treatment center in the DRC's North Kivu province Image: Shi Yu/Xinhua/picture alliance

Congolese authorities officially declared an Ebola outbreak on May 15, but experts believe the virus may have already been circulating for some time before that point.

Officials say it is the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record and is expanding about three times faster than the 2014-2016 outbreak in West Africa — the world's deadliest on record— which killed around 11,000 people.

Ebola is spread between people by direct contact with bodily fluids. It can cause fever, fatigue, and muscle pain, followed by vomiting and diarrhea. Some patients also develop internal or external bleeding.

DRC to receive 70,000 doses of Ervebo Ebola vaccine

Meanwhile, the World Health Organization has announced it will immediately release 70,000 doses of Merck's Ervebo Ebola vaccine to the DRC in a bid to help contain the epidemic.

The Ervebo shot has only been approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, although the WHO said in a statement that early data from animal trials showed it may also give some protection against Bundibugyo — the strain behind the current epidemic.

"The allocation includes 20,000 doses for a Phase 3 clinical trial to understand the impact of the vaccine on the Bundibugyo virus, and 50,000 doses for frontline and health workers," the UN health agency said.

World.title: North Korea: Will Trump-Kim talks happen anytime soon?
World.content:
As Donald Trump claims a meeting is planned with Kim Jong Un, North Korea's response sends a signal that it wants maximum concessions in return for talks with the US.

North Korea responded on Thursday to claims by US President Donald Trump that he will be holding talks with leader Kim Jong Un later in the year with a broadside of ballistic missiles.

The South Korean military said Pyongyang launched 10 short-range missiles that landed in the sea off North Korea's east coast.

This came a day after Kim's powerful sister, Kim Yo Jong, said Pyongyang was "completely unaware of" plans for discussions.

Trump's announcement on Wednesday that he is in contact with Kim and that the two leaders would meet later in the year appears to have caught Pyongyang off guard. It comes after the US president said the military would scale back annual military drills with South Korea.

The statement by Kim Yo Jong, director of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea and one of her brother's closest advisers, dismissed Trump's decision to dramatically scale back the 10-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises as "unworthy of comment and [we] have no interest in it at all."

Kim Yo Jong is known for her fiery rhetoric against the US and South Korea [FILE February 2023] Image: Ahn Young-joon/AP Photo/picture alliance

"After Trump's overtures, Kim Yo Jong effectively said downscaling exercises is not enough, and North Korea launched about a dozen missiles in its third firing in two weeks," Leif-Eric Easley, a professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University in Seoul, told DW.

In a statement carried by the state-run Korea Central News Agency (KCNA), Kim Yo Jong mocked South Korea as a "puppet" and indicated that only canceling the drills in their entirety would be seen as a "goodwill measure."

North Korea's position of power

Choo Jae-woo, a professor of foreign policy at South Korea's Kyung Hee University, told DW that unlike in Trump's first term, Pyongyang right now is in a position of power and will likely seek more guarantees before coming to the negotiating table.

"North Korea is not interested in dialogue because Kim was humiliated in 2019 when Trump walked out of their talks in Hanoi," said Choo said.

Those talks ended in acrimony over the US insistence that North would have to scrap its nuclear program.

Pyongyang has since forged a close security and economic alliance with Russia, granting it access to military technology, energy and consumer goods previously beyond its grasp under international sanctions.

Why North Korea is now Europe's problem To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"They are in the safe hands of Russia and China and, in the years since Hanoi, Kim has made it his regime's official position that North Korea will never engage in dialogue as long as giving up its nuclear weapons is part of the discussion,” Choo added.

Will Trump-Kim talks happen anytime soon?

Easley said that Pyongyang is unlikely to agree to talks with the US, at least in the immediate future.

"North Korea is practically a combatant in a European war, sending ammunition, missiles and soldiers to Russia as it continues to attack Ukraine," he said.

"Kim is benefiting financially from this illegal trade, incorporating new technologies and battlefield experience into his military and industrial base, and receiving Moscow's blessing for de facto nuclear status."

That, in turn, gives Kim leverage to demand greater support from Beijing. Pyongyang is also aware that time is not on Trump's side.

North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump has not yet publicly confirmed a date and venue for talks with Kim, and no agenda has been presented, casting doubt on whether a meeting will take place. The upcoming US midterm elections on November 3 add more political urgency to Trump's timeline.

On the other hand, the North Korean leader may sense that this may be his best opportunity to strike some sort of deal with the US while Trump is still in office.

In her statement earlier this week, Kim Yo Jong said the relationship between Trump and her brother is "still excellent."

Seoul welcomes progress

And while the South Korean government has broadly welcomed Trump's claim that he will meet with Kim later in the year and reiterated that it no longer considers denuclearization of the North a prerequisite for talks, there are concerns among ordinary people in the South, Choo said.

"The fear is that Trump will simply ignore South Korea's security needs and deal directly with North Korea because he is so desperate to get an agreement signed," he said.

"There needs to be close coordination between Seoul and Washington on what is being discussed and agreed because any agreements that are made will affect us far more than the US," he said.

Media reports suggest that the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum on November 18 and 19 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen could provide a suitable venue for Trump and Kim to meet in person.
